newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Crowds seek boat out of rebel-held Albanian port. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Crowds seek boat out of rebel-held Albanian port. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]

text.p: Rebel gunmen fired shots in the air on Saturday to drive off a crowd of pushing and shoving people trying to board the lone ferry still operating from this embattled southern Albanian port.
Several hundred people swarmed around the "Kaliopi" when it arrived with supplies from the nearby Greek island of Corfu on Saturday. The ferry can carry around 100 people.
The rebels fired warning shots to drive the crowd back so supplies could be unloaded and three people wounded in a gunfight with suspected secret police on Friday could be evacuated.
Three rebels were wounded, two seriously, when a car with three men ran their checkpoint in Jara, just inside the Greek border south of Sarande.
Arkadi Loula, a surgeon at Sarande hospital, said one man was shot in the head and foot, the other in the stomach. They were being taken to Corfu for treatment.
The rebels said the men in the car were secret police who were scouting the area for a possible move by the Albanian army to regain control of Sarande and other towns.

Rebels seized Sarande, Delvine, Tepelene (corrects from Telepene) and other towns and villages in anti-government rioting last week against President Sali Berisha and his handling of the collapse of five fraudulent pyramid investment schemes in January.
The rebels seized large stocks of guns from state arsenals, including artillery pieces and tanks, and joined in the popular uprising which started in the port city of Vlore further north.

Rebels in Tepelene have set up headquarters in the town hall and council meetings to coordinate efforts to resist government troops. The army has vanished since getting a bloody nose in a fight with rebels near Delvine, east of Sarande, on Wednesday.
Weapons in Tepelene were being taken away from children and roadblocks set up at every exit.

Outside the home of a teenager who was shot dead -- either by accident or in an exchange of fire at a roadblock -- two Kalashnikov rifles were tied together, a message from his family to Berisha that the boy's death would be avenged.
After days of wild celebrations and constant blasting away in the air by jubilant gunmen, Sarande was quieter on Saturday with ex-army officers taking charge and organising the rebels.

"There will be no more shooting without reason. Parents will take weapons away from kids under 18. The shops will open and there is nothing to fear," Davar, a former army colonel who now controls this southern port, told a crowd of 3,000 on Friday.
He turned down an offer by Berisha for the rebels to put down their weapons by Sunday in return for amnesty.
As the ex-officers showed young rebels how to dig in on hilltops, set up radio links, and camouflage heavy guns, women rushed to small shops to stock up on bread, eggs and milk.
With the regular army controlling a junction linking Sarande with the main north-south road, the town's only supply route is Corfu, a one-hour ride by boat.

Shops were half empty and filling stations close to running out of petrol. Schools were closed and the "rebel council" made up of former officers, policemen and municipal officials imposed a night curfew for security reasons.
